subtopic_detail: Two witnessed breathing pauses at home in a seven week old with mild work of breathing and oxygen saturation of 94 per cent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a seven week old boy, born at thirty five weeks gestation, on day three of a coryzal illness. His parents describe two episodes at home in which he went quiet, stopped breathing for what they estimate was fifteen seconds and looked dusky around the mouth, each ending when they picked him up and rubbed his back.

He has taken about two thirds of his usual feed volume over the past twelve hours. In the department he is alert between examinations and has had no further episode in the ninety minutes since arrival. His older sister has a cold.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession with no tracheal tug or head bob, widespread fine inspiratory crackles with scattered expiratory wheeze, anterior fontanelle soft, capillary refill two seconds, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with written advice, as his oxygen saturation and work of breathing are both reassuring
options.rationale: This anchors on the respiratory parameters, which are indeed mild, and ignores the finding that actually predicts deterioration in this age group. Apnoea in a young ex preterm infant frequently precedes rather than follows respiratory decompensation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Discharge home after a four hour period of observation in the department with continuous saturation monitoring
options.rationale: A short observation window cannot exclude recurrence, since apnoeas in this illness cluster irregularly and often worsen around days three to five, which is where this infant sits. The absence of an event in ninety minutes carries little predictive value. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen at two litres per kilogram per minute and admit to the ward for monitoring
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants failing low flow oxygen after a trial of around two hours, and this infant does not currently require any supplemental oxygen at a saturation of 94 per cent. Escalating support ahead of need adds feeding interference without treating the apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Perform a full septic screen with lumbar puncture and start intravenous antibiotics pending the culture results
options.rationale: A positive viral swab in an afebrile infant with classical auscultatory findings makes concurrent serious bacterial infection unlikely, and apnoea is explained by the confirmed diagnosis. A septic workup would be driven by fever, toxicity or an unexplained picture rather than by apnoea alone in this context. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Admit for inpatient cardiorespiratory monitoring and feeding support, without supplemental oxygen at present
options.rationale: Witnessed apnoea is an admission criterion in its own right in an infant under about two months corrected, because it is the feature that most strongly predicts the need for respiratory support and is independent of saturation and recession. Prematurity at thirty five weeks and reduced feeding compound that risk, and monitoring rather than oxygen is what this infant currently needs. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is the commonest reason for infant admission in Australia, and most disposition decisions are correctly driven by feeding, work of breathing and oxygen requirement. The important exception is apnoea, which in young infants arises from immature central respiratory control responding to viral infection rather than from airway obstruction, and therefore occurs independently of how severe the chest findings look. Risk is concentrated in infants under six to eight weeks of age, those born preterm, and those with chronic lung or cardiac disease or neuromuscular conditions. Australian practice uses low flow nasal prong oxygen as first line when oxygen is needed, with a saturation target of ninety per cent, reserving high flow for failure of low flow after about two hours. Illness typically peaks on days three to five, so an infant presenting at day three is on the rising limb.
key_points: Witnessed apnoea is an independent admission criterion regardless of saturation or work of breathing
Apnoea reflects immature central respiratory control and is concentrated in young and ex preterm infants
Illness peaks at days three to five, so early presentation means the trajectory is still rising
Low flow nasal prong oxygen is first line with a target saturation of ninety per cent
High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow oxygen after a trial of about two hours
explanation.pearls: Apnoea can be the presenting feature of respiratory syncytial virus infection before any cough or crackles appear, so a young infant with an unexplained apnoeic episode in winter warrants a viral swab even when the chest sounds clear.

subtopic_detail: Worsening stridor and high fever twelve hours after dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline produced no sustained improvement
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a three year old boy who was brought in last night with a barking cough and stridor, given oral dexamethasone and two doses of nebulised adrenaline, and admitted to the short stay unit when his stridor kept returning.

This morning he looks worse. He is sitting forward, is not interested in his mother's phone and has a weak cough that no longer sounds barking. He is fully immunised. Over the past six hours his temperature has climbed and he has become increasingly reluctant to swallow his own secretions, though he is not drooling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor at rest with marked tracheal tug and intercostal recession, toxic appearance, no rash, chest sounds symmetrical with poor air entry throughout
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg and repeat nebulised adrenaline every twenty minutes
options.rationale: Repeating the croup bundle treats subglottic oedema, and the failure of two previous doses to hold is itself the evidence that a different process is operating. Escalating a treatment that has already failed twice delays the airway plan this child needs. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Request an urgent lateral neck radiograph to look for a thumbprint sign before making any airway decision
options.rationale: Imaging a child with a threatened airway moves them away from staff and equipment and can precipitate obstruction through distress and positioning. Even when the film is abnormal it does not change the immediate need for a controlled airway assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Activate the difficult airway team for inspection in theatre and start intravenous flucloxacillin with ceftriaxone
options.rationale: High fever, toxicity, a leucocytosis and stridor unresponsive to steroid and adrenaline describe bacterial tracheitis, in which purulent membrane rather than oedema obstructs the airway and adrenaline therefore cannot work. Management is airway inspection and clearance under controlled conditions alongside antistaphylococcal cover with a third generation cephalosporin. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Start high flow humidified oxygen and observe for a further two hours before escalating care any further
options.rationale: Humidified oxygen has no effect on a membranous obstruction and a two hour observation period in a toxic child with biphasic stridor risks obstruction occurring without an airway plan in place. Deterioration in this condition is characteristically abrupt. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline for presumed anaphylaxis and commence intravenous hydrocortisone and antihistamine
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis produces urticaria, angioedema, wheeze or hypotension with a plausible exposure and evolves over minutes to hours, not across a night with rising fever and inflammatory markers. Fever and a C reactive protein at this level are not features of an allergic airway. (Source: ASCIA: Anaphylaxis guidelines)

explanation.summary: Viral croup is common, responds to corticosteroid within a few hours and to nebulised adrenaline within minutes, and the response to that bundle is diagnostically useful. A child whose stridor does not settle, who becomes toxic, and who develops high fever with a marked leucocytosis has moved outside that diagnosis, and bacterial tracheitis is the condition that occupies that space. It usually follows a viral illness, is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, and obstructs through thick purulent membrane that adrenaline cannot shrink. Epiglottitis remains the other differential but has become rare since Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination, and characteristically produces drooling and a muffled voice with a shorter history. All of these children are managed by minimising distress and arranging airway inspection with senior anaesthetic and ear nose and throat involvement in theatre rather than by examining the throat at the bedside.
key_points: Failure to respond to dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline argues against simple viral croup
Toxicity, high fever and marked leucocytosis point to bacterial tracheitis with a purulent membrane
Adrenaline cannot relieve membranous obstruction, which is why repeat dosing fails
Management is controlled airway inspection in theatre plus antistaphylococcal and gram negative cover
Avoid throat examination, cannulation attempts and imaging trips in any child with a threatened airway
explanation.pearls: In croup the RCH dose of dexamethasone is 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate disease, with 0.6 mg/kg reserved for severe croup, and nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000 rather than a weight based dose, with a minimum three hour observation after the last dose.

subtopic_detail: Quiet chest with a normalising respiratory rate and a rising carbon dioxide after an hour of continuous salbutamol
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a nine year old girl who arrived an hour ago with a severe asthma exacerbation. She has had continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone since arrival.

The nurse calls you because the family think she looks calmer. She is no longer speaking in single words because she is not speaking at all, and she is slumped against her mother rather than sitting upright as she was on arrival. Her mother mentions that she was admitted to intensive care with asthma two winters ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on eight litres per minute of oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Minimal audible wheeze with markedly reduced air entry throughout both lung fields, poor respiratory effort with reducing accessory muscle use, drowsy but rousable to voice
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas shows pH 7.21 (7.32-7.42), carbon dioxide 68 mmHg (41-51), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue the current nebulised therapy and repeat the blood gas in thirty minutes to confirm the trend
options.rationale: This reads the falling respiratory rate and quieter chest as improvement when both are signs of exhaustion and critically reduced air movement. Waiting thirty minutes in a child with this gas invites respiratory arrest. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Reduce the oxygen to maintain saturations between 92 and 94 per cent to avoid suppressing respiratory drive
options.rationale: Hypercapnic drive dependence is a concept from chronic obstructive lung disease in adults and does not apply to acute paediatric asthma, where hypoxia is the immediate threat. Reducing oxygen here would worsen the situation without addressing the obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Arrange an urgent chest radiograph to exclude pneumothorax before escalating to any further pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Pneumothorax is worth considering in deteriorating asthma, but breath sounds are symmetrically reduced rather than unilaterally absent and there is no tracheal shift or cardiovascular collapse. Sending an exhausted hypercapnic child to the radiology department delays definitive escalation. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate and call the intensive care team for urgent review at the bedside
options.rationale: A quiet chest with a falling respiratory rate, drowsiness and a rising carbon dioxide describes imminent respiratory failure, not response to treatment, and this child needs second line intravenous bronchodilation with senior critical care input immediately. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first line intravenous agent in Australian paediatric practice for severe asthma failing inhaled therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma acute)

options.text: Change the prednisolone to intravenous hydrocortisone and add a further dose of nebulised ipratropium bromide
options.rationale: Switching the corticosteroid route offers no additional benefit when oral prednisolone has already been absorbed and neither agent acts fast enough to alter the next fifteen minutes. Additional ipratropium adds little once the initial doses have been given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The most dangerous moment in acute paediatric asthma is the point at which the clinical picture appears to settle, because reduced wheeze, a falling respiratory rate and diminishing accessory muscle use can all mean either improvement or exhaustion. The two are separated by mental state, air entry and gas exchange, and a drowsy child with a quiet chest and a rising carbon dioxide is decompensating. Carbon dioxide in acute asthma normally falls because of hyperventilation, so a normal value is already concerning and a raised value indicates failure. Australian escalation moves from continuous inhaled beta agonist and ipratropium with systemic corticosteroid, to intravenous magnesium sulfate, then to intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline with intensive care involvement. A previous intensive care admission is one of the strongest predictors of a further life threatening episode and should lower the threshold for early escalation.
key_points: A quiet chest means reduced air movement, not resolved bronchospasm, until proven otherwise
Carbon dioxide normally falls in acute asthma, so a normal value is concerning and a raised value is failure
Drowsiness, poor effort and a falling respiratory rate in this setting indicate exhaustion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the first line intravenous escalation with intensive care involvement
A prior intensive care admission markedly raises the risk of a subsequent life threatening episode
explanation.pearls: Salbutamol drives potassium into cells and generates lactate through beta two stimulation, so a raised lactate during continuous nebulisation usually reflects the treatment rather than tissue hypoperfusion and is not by itself a reason to give fluid.

subtopic_detail: Doughy skin with preserved blood pressure and a sodium of 163 in an infant whose formula has been scooped incorrectly
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a five month old boy with four days of vomiting and loose stools. His mother, who has been making up formula from a tin with an unfamiliar scoop, reports that he has had three wet nappies in the past day and has been intermittently irritable then sleepy.

He was born at term and has otherwise been well. He has taken small volumes of formula and water throughout. His weight today is 6.4 kg against 7.0 kg recorded at his four month check.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 164 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, skin with a doughy inelastic feel over the abdomen, capillary refill two seconds centrally, irritable when handled and drowsy when left alone, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 163 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), urea 11.8 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 46 micromol/L (20-50), glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.0), venous pH 7.31 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid management?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride as a rapid bolus, then repeat boluses until the pulse rate normalises
options.rationale: Repeated boluses are the correct approach to shock, but this infant has a preserved blood pressure and a central capillary refill of two seconds, so he is dehydrated rather than shocked. Volume loading a child who is not shocked accelerates the fall in sodium and raises the risk of cerebral oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Rehydrate with 0.9 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 48 hours, aiming to lower the sodium by under 0.5 mmol/L each hour
options.rationale: In hypernatraemic dehydration the brain has generated intracellular osmoles over days, so correcting the sodium faster than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour, or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, draws water into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema and seizures. Spreading the deficit and maintenance over 48 hours with an isotonic fluid achieves that rate, with the sodium rechecked frequently. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Rehydrate with 0.45 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 12 hours to correct the deficit promptly
options.rationale: This combines a hypotonic fluid with a short correction window, which is the fastest route to a dangerous fall in serum sodium. The tonicity of the fluid and the duration of the infusion both need to oppose rapid correction rather than accelerate it. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give oral rehydration solution by nasogastric tube at maintenance rate and recheck the electrolytes in 24 hours
options.rationale: Nasogastric rehydration is genuinely first line for mild to moderate dehydration failing oral intake, but a sodium of 163 mmol/L with altered conscious state needs the controlled, measurable correction rate that intravenous therapy provides. A 24 hour interval between electrolyte checks is also too long at this sodium. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)

options.text: Give 3 per cent sodium chloride as a slow infusion to stabilise the sodium before beginning any rehydration
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is used to raise sodium acutely in symptomatic hyponatraemia, which is the opposite disturbance to the one present here. Giving it would worsen an already dangerous hypernatraemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration behaves differently from the isonatraemic form because water is drawn out of cells into the extracellular space, which preserves circulating volume and therefore masks the usual clinical signs. Children look less unwell than their deficit implies, with normal blood pressure and capillary refill, while carrying the characteristic doughy or velvety skin and a fluctuating conscious state. In Australia the commonest causes are gastroenteritis with inadequate free water replacement, and incorrectly reconstituted formula where too much powder is added to too little water. The danger lies in correction, not in the presentation, because the brain generates idiogenic osmoles over days and rapid lowering of serum sodium drives water into brain cells, producing cerebral oedema and seizures. Correction is therefore capped at about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with frequent electrolyte monitoring.
key_points: Extracellular volume is relatively preserved, so clinical signs underestimate the true fluid deficit
Doughy inelastic skin with fluctuating irritability and drowsiness is the characteristic picture
Lower the sodium by no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day
Rehydrate over 48 hours with an isotonic fluid, rechecking electrolytes every four to six hours
Reserve fluid boluses for genuine shock, since volume loading accelerates the fall in sodium
explanation.pearls: A seizure occurring during treatment of hypernatraemic dehydration usually signals that the sodium has fallen too quickly rather than that it remains too high, so the response is to slow or increase the tonicity of the infusion rather than to give more free water.

subtopic_detail: Persisting jaundice at three weeks in a breastfed infant with pale stools and a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a three week old girl brought in because she still looks yellow. She is exclusively breastfed, feeding eight times a day, and her mother is confident about attachment.

Her weight has regained birth weight and is now 200 g above it. Her mother has brought a photograph of this morning's nappy, which shows a putty coloured stool, and mentions that his nappies have looked darker than her older child's did at this age. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, received vitamin K at birth and passed meconium on day one.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced to the abdomen, alert and vigorous, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin with a firm texture, spleen not palpable, no bruising or petechiae, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 212 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 68 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase 384 U/L (less than 50), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.2), full blood count within normal limits, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric liver service the same day for investigation of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
options.rationale: A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L, or above about twenty per cent of the total, is never physiological and never due to breast milk, and with pale stools and a firm liver edge the priority is to exclude biliary atresia. Outcomes after the Kasai portoenterostomy fall sharply beyond sixty days of age, which is what makes the referral same day rather than routine. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Reassure the mother that this is breast milk jaundice and recheck the bilirubin level in a further two weeks
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is common and can persist for up to twelve weeks, but it is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia occurring in a thriving infant with normal stool colour. The conjugated fraction and the pale stool exclude it and a two week delay consumes the window in which surgery works best. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat the total serum bilirubin level in six hours to assess the response
options.rationale: Phototherapy isomerises unconjugated bilirubin and has no effect on the conjugated fraction, so it cannot treat this picture. It is also contraindicated in significant conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia because it can precipitate the bronze baby syndrome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Advise a 24 hour trial of formula feeding and repeat the bilirubin to see whether the level falls appreciably
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding was historically used as a diagnostic manoeuvre for breast milk jaundice and is no longer recommended, since it undermines feeding for a test with poor specificity. It has no role at all once the conjugated fraction is raised. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Arrange a urine sample for culture and treat for urinary tract infection while awaiting the laboratory result
options.rationale: Urinary infection genuinely causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in infancy and a urine culture forms part of the workup, but it does not explain acholic stools or a raised gamma glutamyl transferase of this magnitude. Treating it alone would leave the obstructive process unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Jaundice persisting beyond fourteen days in a term infant, or beyond twenty one days in a preterm infant, requires a split bilirubin rather than reassurance, and that single test determines everything that follows. An unconjugated result in a thriving breastfed baby with normal stools is usually breast milk jaundice, which needs no treatment beyond confirming that the infant is growing and that thyroid screening was normal. A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or above twenty per cent of the total defines neonatal cholestasis and is always pathological. Biliary atresia is the diagnosis that drives the urgency, because it is progressive and because success of the Kasai portoenterostomy declines steeply with age, with the best outcomes before about sixty days. Pale acholic stools and dark urine are the clinical hallmarks, and parents are often better at reporting stool colour than clinicians are at eliciting it.
key_points: Jaundice beyond fourteen days in a term infant requires a split bilirubin, not reassurance
A conjugated fraction above 25 micromol/L or twenty per cent of total is always pathological
Pale acholic stools with dark urine point to obstruction and to biliary atresia specifically
Kasai portoenterostomy outcomes decline sharply beyond about sixty days of age
Phototherapy does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and risks the bronze baby syndrome
explanation.pearls: A normal newborn screening test does not exclude biliary atresia, since the screen detects neither it nor most structural liver disease, so a pale stool at three weeks warrants a split bilirubin regardless of a reassuring heel prick result.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear with a C reactive protein of 62 after apparent improvement on ibuprofen for a presumed irritable hip
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a four year old boy sent back by his general practitioner. He was seen three days ago with a limp after a viral upper respiratory illness, diagnosed with an irritable hip and started on regular ibuprofen, which initially let him walk again.

Since yesterday he has refused to stand at all and cries when his nappy is changed. He has had two brief temperatures at home which his mother recorded as 38.2 and 38.5 degrees Celsius. He has no rash, no history of trauma and no previous joint problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed abducted and externally rotated, pain on any passive internal rotation with involuntary guarding, no effusion palpable, no overlying erythema, log roll of the left hip painless
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h (less than 15), blood culture taken, hip ultrasound shows a 9 mm joint effusion on the right, radiograph of the pelvis shows no bony abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue regular ibuprofen with rest and arrange orthopaedic clinic review in one week if the limp persists
options.rationale: This is the management of transient synovitis, which characteristically improves over a few days rather than progressing to refusal to weight bear with rising inflammatory markers. Anti inflammatory therapy also partially masks the early signs of infection, which is how these presentations are missed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Arrange urgent joint aspiration under image guidance with orthopaedic involvement, before starting antibiotics
options.rationale: Refusal to weight bear, a documented fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and a significant effusion satisfy enough predictive criteria that septic arthritis must be excluded by aspirating the joint. Synovial fluid for Gram stain, cell count and culture is obtained before antibiotics because prior dosing reduces the culture yield that guides later therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous flucloxacillin immediately and review the clinical response over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration compromise the synovial culture and leave the team without an organism to guide a treatment course lasting weeks. A septic hip also needs joint decompression, which antibiotics alone do not provide. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of both hips and pelvis before deciding whether aspiration is warranted here
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for suspected osteomyelitis or when the site is unclear, but here ultrasound has already localised a substantial effusion. In a preschooler it needs anaesthesia and would delay the intervention that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone to settle the synovitis and repeat the inflammatory markers after a 48 hour interval
options.rationale: Corticosteroid would suppress the inflammatory response and the fever while allowing an untreated joint infection to destroy articular cartilage. It has no place until infection has been definitively excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: The central task in the acutely limping child is separating transient synovitis, which is common and self limiting, from septic arthritis, which destroys the joint within days if untreated. The widely used predictive criteria are refusal to weight bear, fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and a white cell count above 12 x10^9/L, with probability of infection rising steeply as more are met. These criteria guide rather than decide, and C reactive protein has since proven the more responsive single marker. A trajectory that worsens after initial improvement on anti inflammatory therapy is a particularly important pattern, because partial treatment softens the early picture. Ultrasound confirms an effusion but cannot distinguish sterile from infected fluid, so aspiration remains the only test that answers the question.
key_points: Predictive criteria are non weight bearing, fever above 38.5, sedimentation rate above 40 and white cells above 12
Ultrasound demonstrates an effusion but cannot distinguish sterile fluid from infected fluid
Aspiration for Gram stain, cell count and culture precedes antibiotics to preserve the microbiological yield
Deterioration after initial improvement on anti inflammatory therapy argues against transient synovitis
Untreated septic arthritis of the hip destroys cartilage and threatens the femoral head blood supply
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of septic arthritis between six months and four years, grows poorly on solid media and is often missed unless synovial fluid is inoculated into blood culture bottles or sent for nucleic acid testing.

subtopic_detail: Headache with a pulse of 62 and a rising blood pressure six hours into treatment as the biochemistry improves
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar overnight, managing an eleven year old girl admitted six hours ago with new onset diabetes. She has been on an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour and on a maintenance plus deficit fluid regimen calculated for eight per cent dehydration over 48 hours.

Her capillary glucose has fallen from 34 to 14 mmol/L and her ketones from 5.8 to 2.1 mmol/L. The nurse calls you because the girl has developed a headache and has vomited once, having been settled and conversational an hour ago. She is now irritable and slow to answer questions, and complains that the overhead light hurts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 62 beats per minute having been 118 on arrival, blood pressure 138/88 mmHg having been 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13 with confused speech, pupils equal at 4 mm and sluggishly reactive, no neck stiffness, no focal limb weakness, no papilloedema visible on fundoscopy
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.28 (7.32-7.42) improved from 7.02, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L (22-32) improved from 8, sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145) with corrected sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.5-7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate to 0.1 units/kg/hour, as the persisting ketonaemia indicates inadequate suppression
options.rationale: The biochemistry is in fact correcting steadily and the ketone fall is appropriate, so the deterioration is not explained by insufficient insulin. Raising the rate would accelerate the osmotic shift that is the likely driver of the neurological change. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride, attributing the bradycardia and confusion to hypovolaemia
options.rationale: Hypovolaemia produces tachycardia with a narrow pulse pressure, not bradycardia with hypertension, so the haemodynamic pattern points the opposite way. A fluid bolus would add to intracranial volume at precisely the wrong moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline or mannitol, reduce the fluid rate by a third and arrange urgent intensive care review
options.rationale: Headache with a falling conscious state, bradycardia and rising blood pressure occurring while the biochemistry improves is cerebral oedema, and the Cushing response means treatment cannot wait for imaging. Hyperosmolar therapy with reduction of the fluid infusion rate and immediate critical care involvement is the intervention that alters outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Arrange an urgent computed tomography scan of the brain and treat according to whatever the imaging demonstrates
options.rationale: Imaging is frequently normal in the early hours of this complication and a transfer to the scanner delays treatment during the period when deterioration is fastest. The diagnosis in this setting is clinical and treatment precedes confirmation. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Add intravenous glucose to the infusion and continue the current regimen, treating this as symptomatic hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Glucose is added to the fluid once the level approaches 14 to 17 mmol/L so that insulin can continue to clear ketones, and that adjustment is indeed due here. It does not account for bradycardia and hypertension, and treating this as hypoglycaemia at a glucose of 14 mmol/L misreads the picture. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema complicates roughly one per cent of paediatric episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis but accounts for the majority of deaths and lasting neurological disability, and it characteristically appears four to twelve hours into treatment, when the numbers are improving and the team has begun to relax. Risk is concentrated in younger children, in new onset diabetes, and in those presenting with more severe acidosis and a higher urea. The warning features are headache, recurrent vomiting, irritability or drowsiness, incontinence, and specific cranial nerve palsies, with bradycardia and hypertension representing the late Cushing response rather than an early sign. A failure of the sodium to rise as the glucose falls is an important biochemical warning, since corrected sodium should climb during treatment. Because computed tomography is often normal early and transfer wastes time, treatment with hyperosmolar therapy is given on clinical grounds.
key_points: Onset is typically four to twelve hours into treatment, as the biochemistry is improving
Bradycardia with rising blood pressure is a late Cushing response, not a sign of hypovolaemia
Risk concentrates in younger children, new onset diabetes and more severe presenting acidosis
Treat clinically with hypertonic saline or mannitol and reduced fluid rate rather than awaiting imaging
A corrected sodium that fails to rise as glucose falls is an early biochemical warning sign
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium rises by about 2.4 mmol/L for every 5.5 mmol/L fall in glucose, so plotting it hourly during treatment gives an objective early warning that precedes any change in conscious state.
